html:
The Macedonian dynasty ruled the Byzantine Empire from 867 to 1056. Under it the empire reached its greatest extent since the Arab conquests, and enjoyed a revival of learning and art.

Its founder, Basil I, was a peasant's son from the province of Macedonia, in Thrace, who rose as a groom and favourite of Michael III and then murdered him. His line lasted almost two centuries:

  • Leo VI (886 to 912), who completed the law code begun by his father;
  • Constantine VII (913 to 959), a scholar emperor, long kept in the shadow of the admiral Romanos Lekapenos;
  • the soldier emperors Nikephoros II Phokas and John Tzimiskes, who ruled for the young heirs and retook Crete, Cyprus and Antioch;
  • Basil II (976 to 1025), who conquered Bulgaria after his victory at Kleidion in 1014;
  • the sisters Zoe and Theodora, through whom later emperors ruled by marriage or adoption, until Theodora died in 1056.

The Macedonian emperors replaced the old Ecloga with new law books, and their era saw great encyclopedias, illuminated books and mosaics such as those of Hosios Loukas. Fifteen years after the dynasty ended, the empire lost most of Anatolia after the Battle of Manzikert.
sum: The Macedonian dynasty ruled the Byzantine Empire from 867 to 1056. Under it the empire reached its greatest extent since the Arab conquests, and enjoyed a revival of learning and art.
